criteria.quote: Zapdos appears only when a thundercloud splits in two.
criteria.revision: Open with the contrast, not just the rule: "Zapdos lives in thunderclouds, controls electricity—and is said to appear only when one splits in two."

criteria.quote: Zapdos is said to live in thunderclouds and control electricity.
If Zapdos lives in thunderclouds and causes storms, why require a split?
criteria.revision: Move this question into the opening narration and make the evidence explicit: "Zapdos lives in thunderclouds and causes storms—so why do two Pokédex entries say it appears only when a thundercloud splits in two?"

criteria.quote: Two entries give one precise condition: a thundercloud parts in two.
criteria.revision: Replace the repeated condition with a new contrast from the entries: "Other entries link Zapdos's appearance to dark skies and lightning showers. But Silver and SoulSilver add the unusually specific split-cloud condition."

Delay the split-cloud reveal until after the storm evidence. After the thundercloud habitat and storm-making lines, reveal: "But two entries give its appearance a stranger condition: the thundercloud must part into two halves."

criteria.quote: Zapdos appears only when a thundercloud splits in two.
criteria.revision: Cut or replace the later repetitions, especially "The bird that causes storms has the strangest arrival rule." Use the unused evidence instead: "One entry says it appears when the sky turns dark and lightning showers down; two others specify the cloud splitting in two."

criteria.quote: Zapdos causes storms, yet appears only after one exact sky change.
criteria.revision: Make the ending resolve the contrast rather than restate it: "The strange part isn't that Zapdos belongs to storms—it's that two entries make the cloud's shape, not just darkness or lightning, part of its arrival rule."

criteria.quote: Better entrance: arriving with lightning, or splitting a thundercloud?
criteria.revision: End on the evidence-based interpretive split: "Is the split-cloud line just a more specific version of Zapdos's storm arrival—or a genuinely different rule?"

findings.quote: Zapdos is said to live in thunderclouds and control electricity.
findings.note: 2 of 4 middle scenes read as stat statements ("It is…", "It has…"). Turn them into steps of one argument: each scene should answer "so what?" about the previous one.
